body:
Folk dance as living cultural heritage

Folk dances are traditional forms of collective artistic expression that develop within communities and are transmitted from one generation to another. They reflect religious beliefs, occupations, local environments, social customs and collective celebrations.

In Gujarat, folk dances form an important part of festivals, religious ceremonies, marriages and village fairs. Although circular formations, rhythmic singing and percussion instruments are common, different communities have developed distinctive dance traditions.

Major folk dance traditions of Gujarat

The principal forms can be understood through their cultural associations.

  • Religious devotion: Garba expresses devotion to Shakti, while Raas is closely associated with Krishna and his Raas Leela.
  • Occupational life: Tippani reflects the labour of women engaged in construction work, Hudo reflects pastoral life, and Padhar dance reflects the experiences of fishing and boating communities.
  • Community and tribal traditions: Siddi Dhamal preserves elements of African-origin cultural heritage within Gujarat, while Dangi dances express the collective traditions of the tribal communities of Dang.

These associations are not mutually exclusive. An occupational dance may also be performed during religious festivals, and a religious dance may become a widely shared social celebration.

Common musical instruments

InstrumentNature
DholTraditional percussion drum
DholakDouble-headed drum
ManjiraPair of small metallic cymbals
ThaliMetal plate struck to produce rhythm
ShehnaiReed-based wind instrument
PavriTraditional tribal wind instrument

Dance props can also produce rhythm. For example, dandiya sticks produce sound when struck together, while the Tippani implement produces a rhythmic sound when struck against the ground.

Identifying a folk dance

The most useful identifying features are its traditional community, geographical association, occasion and distinctive instrument or prop. A common instrument such as the dhol may accompany several different dances and is therefore not sufficient by itself to identify one particular form.

Prelims focus

  • Garba is principally associated with Shakti worship.
  • Raas is closely associated with Krishna devotion.
  • Tippani developed from manual labour.
  • Hudo reflects pastoral life.
  • Padhar dance reflects fishing and boating traditions.
  • Dhamal and Dangi dances have distinctive community associations.

[References: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicraft and Fine Arts, pp. 15–16; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Gujarat, Table 1, pp. 38–39; Utpala Desai, Raas Traditions of Gujarat, Sahapedia; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, ADI KALAKAR Portal, Pawari Dance. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]

title: Gujarat's Folk Dance Traditions and Their Cultural Significance

body:
Meaning and religious significance

Garba is a traditional ritualistic and devotional folk dance of Gujarat, particularly associated with the worship of the feminine divine power known as Shakti.

The name is traditionally derived from Garbha Deep, meaning a lamp within a womb-like enclosure. A perforated earthen pot containing a lighted oil lamp is an important traditional symbol of Garba. The lamp represents life and divine energy.

Participants generally dance around the illuminated pot, a central shrine or an image of the mother goddess Amba, also worshipped as Jagdamba.

Occasion and performance

Garba is celebrated throughout Gujarat, particularly during the 9 nights of Sharad Navratri in the Hindu month of Aso, also called Ashwin. The principal festive period extends from the first to the ninth day of the bright fortnight of this month. In some places, related celebrations continue until the tenth day or take place on Sharad Purnima.

  • Dancers generally move in a circle around a central sacred object.
  • Traditional Garba commonly proceeds in an anticlockwise direction.
  • Rhythm is maintained through singing, handclapping and drumbeats.
  • Common accompanying instruments include the dhol, dholak and manjira.
  • Traditional clothing includes chaniya-choli for women and kediyu with traditional lower garments for men.

Women have historically played a prominent role in Garba, but contemporary Garba is widely performed by both men and women. It is not restricted to a single caste, tribe or district.

Garba and Garbi

Traditional Navratri Garba is principally associated with the worship of the Mother Goddess. Garbi is also an important Gujarati devotional poetic and performance tradition, with a strong association with Krishna Bhakti.

The Gujarati devotional poet Dayaram is particularly remembered for his Garbis expressing love and devotion towards Krishna from the perspective of the Gopis. The distinction concerns important traditional devotional themes rather than an absolute separation between all Garba and Garbi songs.

UNESCO recognition in 2023

On 6 December 2023, UNESCO inscribed Garba of Gujarat on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

AspectFact
Official name of the elementGarba of Gujarat
Date of inscription6 December 2023
UNESCO committee session18th session
VenueKasane, Botswana
Governing convention2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage
ListRepresentative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity
Position at inscription15th Indian element to be inscribed
Decision number18.COM 8.b.32
Nomination number01962

Garba of Gujarat had already been included in India's National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2022. This inventory is maintained by the Sangeet Natak Akademi.

What UNESCO recognition means

Intangible cultural heritage includes living practices, knowledge, skills, rituals and performing arts inherited and maintained by communities. UNESCO's recognition of Garba acknowledges a living cultural tradition rather than a physical monument or archaeological site.

The inscription encourages safeguarding, intergenerational transmission and public awareness of the tradition. It also recognises Garba's contribution to collective participation and social inclusion.

As of 25 November 2026, Garba of Gujarat remains inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List. Its position as India's 15th inscription refers specifically to the time of its inscription in December 2023, not to the current total number of Indian elements.

Intangible heritage is not World Heritage

Garba was recognised under the 2003 Intangible Cultural Heritage Convention. It was not designated as a physical UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the inscription did not separately designate Dandiya Raas.

Prelims focus

  • Garba is associated with Garbha Deep and Shakti worship.
  • Dayaram is particularly associated with Krishna-devotional Garbis.
  • Garba of Gujarat was inscribed on 6 December 2023.
  • The decision was taken at the 18th committee session in Kasane, Botswana.
  • Garba was India's 15th inscription at the time.
  • Trap: The recognition concerns intangible cultural heritage, not the World Heritage List.

[References: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, pp. 15–16; UNESCO, Garba of Gujarat, nomination 01962; UNESCO, Decision 18.COM 8.b.32; UNESCO, Garba of Gujarat Inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, 6 December 2023; Ministry of Culture, Press Information Bureau, Garba of Gujarat Declared as Intangible Cultural Heritage by UNESCO, 6 December 2023; UNESCO, India, Listing of Intangible Cultural Heritage. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Garbha Deep and the circular Garba tradition.

title: Garba: Shakti Worship and UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

body:
Meaning and devotional background

Raas, also written as Rasa, is a traditional Gujarati group dance involving rhythmic movements, singing and coordinated formations. It is commonly associated with Krishna's Raas Leela, the devotional tradition of Krishna dancing with the Gopis of Vrindavan.

The popularity of Raas in Gujarat is closely connected with the spread of Vaishnava devotional traditions. Gujarati religious literature and oral traditions helped transmit stories of Krishna and the Raas Leela.

A traditional devotional account associated with the Gujarati saint-poet Narsinh Mehta describes Krishna granting him a vision of the Raas Leela. This is a religious tradition rather than a historically established account of the invention of Raas.

Dandiya Raas

Dandiya Raas is a prominent form of Raas in which participants use short sticks called dandiya to produce rhythmic sounds while dancing.

It is especially associated with Saurashtra and Kachchh, although it is now performed throughout Gujarat and among Gujarati communities outside the state.

  • Occasions: Navratri, Janmashtami, fairs and weddings.
  • Participants: Men and women, depending on the particular community and tradition.
  • Distinctive prop: Dandiya sticks.
  • Accompaniment: Dhol, tabla, harmonium and other locally available instruments.

Dandiya Raas is one form of Raas. Other traditions use handclapping, manjira or earthen pots. Therefore, the use of sticks should not be treated as a compulsory feature of every form of Raas.

Garba and Raas compared

FeatureGarbaRaas
Principal devotional associationShakti and Mother GoddessKrishna and Raas Leela
Main occasionsNavratriNavratri and Janmashtami
Typical rhythmic featureHandclapping and singingSticks or other rhythmic accompaniments
Characteristic traditional objectIlluminated earthen potDandiya sticks in Dandiya Raas
Regional distributionThroughout GujaratStrong traditions in Saurashtra and Kachchh; now widespread
UNESCO inscriptionGarba of Gujarat, 2023Not separately inscribed as Raas

Both dances are performed during Navratri, and both may use circular formations and drumbeats. Their principal devotional associations and characteristic objects provide more reliable distinctions than the festival or formation alone.

Community-specific forms of Raas

Raas developed into distinct regional and occupational traditions. Two important examples are Hudo Raas, associated particularly with the Bharwad pastoral community, and Padhar Raas, associated with the fishing and boating traditions of the Padhar community.

Prelims focus

  • Raas is traditionally associated with Krishna and Raas Leela.
  • Navratri and Janmashtami are important occasions for Raas.
  • Dandiya Raas uses short rhythmic sticks.
  • Hudo Raas has a pastoral community association.
  • Padhar Raas has a fishing and boating community association.
  • Trap: Not all Raas traditions require dandiya sticks.

[References: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, pp. 15–16; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Gujarat, Table 1, p. 38; Utpala Desai, Raas Traditions of Gujarat, Sahapedia, Introduction and Community-based Classification; District Kachchh, Government of Gujarat, Kachchh Folk Dances; UNESCO, Garba of Gujarat, nomination 01962. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Raas is a Krishna-associated family including Dandiya, Hudo and Padhar Raas; dandiya sticks are not required in every tradition.
pictures.caption: Dandiya Raas is one form within the wider Raas tradition.

title: Raas and Dandiya Raas: Krishna Devotion and Regional Traditions

body:
Tippani dance

Tippani is a traditional female-dominated folk dance of Saurashtra, particularly associated with the Chorwad–Veraval coastal belt. Chorwad is in Junagadh district, while Veraval is in Gir Somnath district.

The dance developed from the traditional construction practice of compacting lime-based floors and foundations. Women performing this physically demanding work used a wooden implement called a Tippani. By singing and striking the ground in a common rhythm, they reduced the monotony of collective labour.

Over time, this rhythmic occupational activity developed into a distinct folk dance performed independently of construction work.

Community and identifying features

  • Communities: Particularly associated with Koli and Kharva women of coastal Saurashtra. Bhil and several other working communities also have Tippani traditions.
  • Traditional participants: Predominantly women.
  • Occasions: Weddings, festivals and cultural programmes.
  • Distinctive implement: A long wooden handle fitted with a wooden or iron block at its lower end.
  • Accompaniment: Dhol, manjira, thali, tabla and shehnai may accompany the rhythmic striking of the ground.

The block attached to the implement is also known as a Gadbo. The weighted lower end helps produce the characteristic impact against the ground.

Tippani differs from Dandiya Raas because its characteristic action involves striking a long implement against the ground, whereas Dandiya Raas commonly involves striking short sticks together.

Hudo dance

Hudo, also called Hudo Raas, is a vigorous folk dance particularly associated with the Bharwad community, whose traditional occupation is sheep and cattle rearing.

The dance is traditionally understood to imitate the movements of sheep or rams confronting one another. Its characteristic rhythmic clapping and energetic movements reflect the pastoral environment in which it developed.

Community and geographical association

Hudo is strongly associated with the Panchal region, particularly Tarnetar and surrounding villages in Surendranagar district. The Bharwads are its principal traditional community, although Rabari and Koli groups also perform related traditions.

Occasions and instruments

  • Hudo is performed during weddings, fairs and social celebrations.
  • The Tarnetar Fair is particularly famous for Hudo performances.
  • Both men and women traditionally participate.
  • Rhythmic handclapping is a distinctive feature.
  • Common accompanying instruments include the dhol, dholak, manjira, harmonium and flute.

The social context of the Tarnetar Fair includes traditional matchmaking among participating communities. Hudo forms part of the collective celebrations associated with this gathering.

Occupational associations

Tippani represents the collective labour of women engaged in construction and floor preparation. Hudo represents the pastoral traditions of shepherds, particularly the Bharwads.

Prelims focus

  • Tippani is a predominantly female folk dance.
  • Tippani is associated with the Chorwad–Veraval coastal region of Saurashtra.
  • The Tippani implement is struck against the ground.
  • Hudo is principally associated with the Bharwad community.
  • Hudo is associated with the Tarnetar Fair of Surendranagar district.
  • Trap: The movement inspired by sheep fights belongs to Hudo, not Tippani.

[References: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, p. 15; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Gujarat, Table 1, p. 38; The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Bharatiya Lok Kalakar, ISBN 978-81-956774-1-2, pp. 215–216; Gujarat Tourism, Tarnetar Fair, festival account published in The Week Plus, 25 December 2011; District Junagadh, Government of Gujarat, City Survey Offices; District Surendranagar, Government of Gujarat, Tarnetar Fair. Online sources consulted on 25 November 2026.]
